title: Hari Singh Nalwa
hookLine: his great general held the north-west frontier and died at Jamrud
tomorrow: The Maharaja at the Akal Takht

cards: Rocky hills. A narrow pass climbing west into the mountains: the Khyber. At its mouth stands a fort called Jamrud, and inside it a small garrison is waiting for a fight.

Somewhere in the hills an army is coming down. The man responsible for this edge of the kingdom is a general whose name, the stories say, had become a word for nerve. When he falls, the fort still has to hold.

teach.h: NALWA: A NAME FROM A TIGER STORY.
teach.b: First, the name. Tradition explains Nalwa with a story: on a hunt, a tiger sprang at the young Hari Singh, and he fought it and killed it. Whether every detail is true or not, the name stuck to him like armor.
Ranjit Singh's kingdom reached toward the mountains of the north-west, toward Peshawar and the Khyber.

That edge was hard to hold: rough country, local powers with their own claims, and a kingdom in Kabul that claimed the same ground. Hari Singh Nalwa was sent to hold it. He governed, built forts and kept the passes.
Then Jamrud. Tradition tells it like this. An Afghan army came down to the fort.
Hari Singh rode out to relieve it and was mortally wounded in the fighting.

As he lay dying, he asked his men to keep his death a secret, so that defenders and enemy alike would think he was still in command until help could arrive. They did, and tradition says the fort held.

teach.h: THE HERO NEVER LEAVES THE FIELD.
teach.b: In the Guru Granth Sahib, Kabir says the true hero is the one who fights for the deen, a word some read as the helpless and some as the faith, and who would be cut to pieces before leaving the field.
Some Sikhs hear that line in stories like this one.
The story honors not glory or the size of the battle, but a man who stood at the edge so others could live behind it, and who even in dying thought about who would hold the line.

how: Sikhs tell stories of Hari Singh Nalwa as a general of great courage, and some connect his story with Kabir's verse about the true hero who never leaves the field.

games.q: you're the general, mortally wounded near Jamrud. the fort is under attack and help hasn't arrived. what do you ask of your men?
o: tell everyone at once that you're dying.
abandon the fort and save themselves.
keep your death a secret until help arrives.
games.why: tradition says he asked them to hide his death, so the line would hold. they did, and the fort held.

practice: Bring to mind the people who count on you right now, someone at home, a friend, a team, a class, and then your worst kind of day, tired and short on patience.
Name plainly the one thing you would still do for them on that day, and feel your feet on the floor while you hold it; if you pray, Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Nalwa, the name a tiger fight gave Hari Singh, Ranjit Singh's general on the north-west frontier, who died at Jamrud and, tradition says, kept the fort holding even then. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi for Hari Singh Nalwa, Ranjit Singh's general on the north-west frontier.

carryVoice: Your line: the frontier held. A name that meant nerve. That's day nine hundred fourteen.
